# SQL Injection in Plain English: When User Input Rewrites Your Query

SQL injection is the oldest bug on most AppSec lists, and it still turns up in code review. The idea is simple: your app builds a database query by gluing text together, and part of that text came from a user. If the user's text contains SQL, the database can't tell where your query ends and theirs begins.

MITRE files it as [CWE-89](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/89.html) ("Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command"). OWASP's Top 10:2025 groups it under [A05:2025 Injection](https://owasp.org/Top10/2025/A05_2025-Injection/) and counts more than 14k CVEs for SQL injection alone. Long names, same problem: data got treated as code.

## What it looks like in a Java 8 app

Here's the classic version, straight from the [OWASP SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/SQL_Injection_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html):

```java
String query = "SELECT account_balance FROM user_data WHERE user_name = "
             + request.getParameter("customerName");
Statement statement = connection.createStatement();
ResultSet results = statement.executeQuery(query);
```

Send `tom' or '1'='1` instead of a name and the WHERE clause matches every row. CWE-89's examples take the same trick further: reading other users' rows, and on databases that allow stacked statements, `'; DELETE FROM items; --`.

Hibernate doesn't make it go away. HQL and JPQL (the object-flavored query languages Hibernate and JPA use) have the same bug when you build them with `+`. MITRE even has a child entry for it, [CWE-564 "SQL Injection: Hibernate"](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/564.html):

```java
session.createQuery("from Inventory where productID='" + userSuppliedParameter + "'");
```

## The fix: placeholders, not glue

Parameterized queries (also called prepared statements or bind variables) flip the order. You write the whole SQL first with `?` or `:name` holes, then hand the values over separately. The database settles the shape of the query before it sees the value, so `tom' or '1'='1` is just a weird username that matches nobody.

Plain JDBC:

```java
PreparedStatement ps = connection.prepareStatement(
    "SELECT account_balance FROM user_data WHERE user_name = ?");
ps.setString(1, custname);
```

Spring's [`JdbcTemplate`](https://docs.spring.io/spring-framework/reference/data-access/jdbc/core.html) does the same with less ceremony. The values go in as trailing arguments:

```java
int count = jdbcTemplate.queryForObject(
    "select count(*) from t_actor where first_name = ?", Integer.class, firstName);
```

`NamedParameterJdbcTemplate` (`:first_name`) and Spring 6.1's `JdbcClient` (`.param(...)`) do the same thing with names.

On the JPA side, HQL/JPQL uses `:productid` plus `setParameter("productid", value)`. In [Spring Data JPA](https://docs.spring.io/spring-data/jpa/reference/jpa/query-methods.html), derived queries like `findByEmailAddress(String email)` are bound for you, and `@Query("select u from User u where u.emailAddress = ?1")` binds `?1` or `:name` the same way. So does `@NativeQuery` / `@Query(nativeQuery = true)`.

## The trap: PreparedStatement isn't the fix, the `?` is

```java
connection.prepareStatement("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + name + "'");
```

That's a PreparedStatement, and it's still injectable. The class name doesn't matter. What matters is whether the user's value went into the SQL string or into a bind slot. The same goes for `jdbcTemplate.query("... where name = '" + name + "'", mapper)`.

## Where it hides during a strangler replacement

When you carve a section out of the Java 8 monolith and rebuild it in Spring Boot behind an Angular front end, the risky move is porting the old DAO's query-building code "as-is, so behavior stays identical."

A Spring Data `@Query` string has to be a compile-time constant ([a Java annotation rule](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se21/html/jls-9.html#jls-9.7.1)), so you can't glue request input into it directly. That's good. It also means the old concatenation tends to land right next to it: a custom repository method calling `entityManager.createNativeQuery(sql + filter)`, or a `JdbcTemplate` call with a hand-built WHERE clause. It sits in a fresh Spring Boot service with constructor injection and unit tests, and it reads like modern code. It isn't.

Review rule of thumb for the new side: every user value arrives as a method argument and lands on a `?` or `:name`. Never as a piece of a string.

## What GitLab SAST flags, and how to read the Jira ticket

GitLab's [standard SAST](https://docs.gitlab.com/user/application_security/sast/) for Java runs a Semgrep-based analyzer with GitLab-managed rules. The SQL rule ([`java_inject_rule-SqlInjection`](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/security-products/sast-rules/-/blob/main/rules/lgpl-cc/java/inject/rule-SqlInjection.yml), CWE-89, severity High) is a taint rule. "Taint" just means it follows data from where it enters to where it gets used. Sources include servlet request getters, file and socket reads, Jackson `readValue`, and any `String` method parameter. It tracks them through `+`, `concat`, `StringBuilder.append`, and `String.format`, and flags them when they reach sinks like `Statement.executeQuery`, `Connection.prepareStatement`, `JdbcTemplate.query`/`update`/`queryForObject`, Hibernate `createQuery`/`createSQLQuery`, and `EntityManager.createQuery`/`createNativeQuery`.

So when the finding lands in Jira:

1. **Go to the sink line.** If the SQL argument was built with `+`, `append`, or `format` from anything that isn't a constant, treat it as real.
2. **Make the fix mechanical.** Move the value to a placeholder and pass it as an argument. Don't "fix" it with escaping. OWASP marks escaping as strongly discouraged because it's database-specific and fragile.
3. **Shrink the blast radius anyway.** The app's database account shouldn't be DBA or owner. OWASP and CWE-89 both push least privilege, so one missed query can't read or drop everything.

## The short version

SQL injection happens when user text becomes part of the SQL instead of a value handed to it. In Java and Spring Boot the fix is boring: PreparedStatement with `?`, JdbcTemplate with trailing arguments, `:name` parameters in JPQL/HQL and `@Query`. Watch the strangler port, where old string-built queries move into new-looking Spring Boot code, and use GitLab SAST's taint findings to go straight to the sink you need to fix.
chris_take_options: A: Here's the counterintuitive one: the javax-to-jakarta rename in Spring Boot 3 can make the scan quieter without making the code any safer. GitLab's public Semgrep rule for Java SQL injection still lists its EntityManager sinks under javax.persistence, so before I trust a clean scan on a freshly strangled slice, I push one deliberately bad createNativeQuery("..." + name) to a throwaway branch and make sure a Jira ticket actually shows up.

B: The triage trade-off I actually live with: I tag every SQL injection ticket by which side of the strangler it's on. Old-side findings in code that's already scheduled for deletion get a dated risk acceptance tied to the cutover, and new-side findings block the merge request. Otherwise the team burns a sprint parameterizing a DAO that won't exist next quarter while the new service quietly picks up the same pattern.

C: I fix some SQL that SAST never flags. GitLab's rule only treats String method parameters as tainted, so a controller taking a Long orderId and doing "... where id = " + orderId scans clean. That Long is the only thing protecting the query, and it lasts exactly until someone changes the DTO field to String to support legacy IDs with letters in them. That diff looks like a type tweak, not a SQL change, so I'd rather move it to a ? now.
